preamble: Fronting of the close back rounded vowel [u(ː)] to the close central rounded [ʉ(ː)]. In the Late Old Swedish vowel shift (stora vokaldansen), long [uː] became [ʉː], as in hūs [huːs] > hus [hʉːs] 'house', while [oː] was raised to [uː] and [aː] to [oː]. Many Norwegian dialects share the change (Old Norse hús > hus /hʉːs/), but Danish does not. In Swedish, Old Norse short u that stayed short became the lower short [ɵ] instead (fullr > full /fɵl/), listed under u → ɵ. In many accents of English the GOOSE vowel /uː/ is fronted to [ʉː] (GOOSE-fronting), as in Australian and New Zealand goose /ɡʉːs/; present-day Received Pronunciation has also fronted it, to about [ʉː] with reduced lip-rounding. Russian has the same quality as an allophone: stressed /u/ is centralized to [ʉ] between palatalized consonants, as in чуть [t͡ɕʉtʲ] 'barely'; Wikipedia gives the rule after Jones & Ward (1969). Yanushevskaya & Bunčić (2015) describe the same fronting, strongest between palatalized consonants, but transcribe the vowel as advanced back [u̟], as in люки [ˈl̠ʲu̟ˑkʲɪ] 'hatches'.

examples.from: Old Swedish mūs 'mouse' (< Old Norse mús)
examples.note: Part of the Late Old Swedish vowel shift, in which [oː] became [uː] (bōk > bok [buːk]) and [aː] became [oː] (blā > blå [bloː]). In Central Standard Swedish the vowel is now near-close near-front [ʏː] (Engstrand 1990, cited by Wikipedia), but it is still written /ʉː/.

examples.from: Early Modern English goose /uː/ (< Middle English /oː/; traditional RP /ɡuːs/)

examples.note: The RP article reports the same fronting of GOOSE to [ʉː] in present-day RP (Collins and Mees 2013). New Zealand English retracts the vowel to [uː] before /l/, so too [tʰʉː] differs from tool [tʰuːl].
Yanushevskaya & Bunčić (2015) write the vowel after soft /lʲ/ as advanced back [u̟]: люки [ˈl̠ʲu̟ˑkʲɪ] 'hatches', against luk [ˈɫ̪uˑk] 'onion'.
Unstressed /u/ in the same position is near-close [ʉ̞], as in ютиться [jʉ̞ˈtʲitsə] 'to huddle'; elsewhere unstressed /u/ is [ʊ].
